questions.question: Is Go map iteration order random?
questions.title: Is Go Map Iteration Order Random
questions.direct_answer: Deliberately — the runtime randomizes the start so no code can rely on order. Sort the keys when order matters.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Map Iteration And Nil beyond memorized syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving a definition without explaining a practical trade-off.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Deliberately — the runtime randomizes the start so no code can rely on order. Sort the keys when order matters.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Deep Dive
sections.content:
The randomness lives in the map iterator's initialization: a Go map is a hash table with buckets in a fixed layout, but the iterator selects its starting bucket and intra-bucket offset pseudo-randomly per iteration. Same map, same layout, different starting point — so the visit order differs every time.

Why the runtime pays for this deliberately: before randomization (pre-Go-1.0), map order was deterministic for a given insert sequence. Programs that only worked by that accident passed all their tests and shipped. The Go team flipped it to randomized so that any such dependency breaks loudly and immediately in development rather than quietly in production. It's a rare case of a runtime adding chaos as a correctness feature.

The sorted-keys pattern is the canonical alternative, and it's what the standard library's own tools do when they need determinism (text/template's sorted key iteration, flag's Visit using sorted lexicographic order). One allocation for the key slice, one sort, and the iteration order becomes a property of the data rather than of the hash seeds.

questions.question: What is the comma-ok idiom for maps?
questions.title: Comma-ok Idiom For Maps
questions.direct_answer: v, ok := m[key] — ok is true only when the key exists. It distinguishes a stored zero value from a missing key.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: v, ok := m[key] — ok is true only when the key exists. It distinguishes a stored zero value from a missing key.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Deep Dive
sections.content:
Mechanically, the comma-ok lookup is the same hash-table probe as the one-value form; the runtime additionally reports whether the probe found a bucket entry. The mapaccess operations return both pieces; the single-value form just discards the boolean.

The idiom generalizes beyond maps — Go uses comma-ok wherever a bare value is ambiguous:

- type assertions: `x, ok := i.(string)` — ok false instead of panic
- channel receive: `v, ok := <-ch` — ok false means closed
- function with ok: `strconv.Atoi`-style pairs

In every case, the pattern answers the same design question: 'the zero value of this type is also a valid in-band value, so success needs its own channel.' Learning comma-ok on maps is the entry point to a convention that spans the language — and recognizing when a bare value can't distinguish your cases is the skill.

The interview-ready framing: maps are total functions — every key gives an answer. When absence itself is information, you need the ok channel. When the default answer suffices, the one-value form keeps the code to what matters.

questions.question: How do you delete from a map, and is it safe if the key is missing?
questions.title: Elete From A Map, And Is It
questions.direct_answer: delete(m, key) — safe on any key, including missing ones, and on nil maps. No error, no return value.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Map Iteration And Nil.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: delete(m, key) — safe on any key, including missing ones, and on nil maps. No error, no return value.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Deletion is a one-way, no-feedback operation:

```go
delete(m, "stale-key")
```

There's no return value, no error, and no effect if the key doesn't exist. Deleting a missing key is a no-op, not a failure — the runtime probes for the entry and, finding none, does nothing. The same call works on a nil map without panic: probe nothing, do nothing.

That silence is the design question. Deletion being total (works on any input) means you never guard it — no 'if _, ok := m[k]; ok { delete(m, k) }' dance; just delete. But the flip side is you can't tell from the call whether anything happened. If you need 'was it there?', capture that with a lookup first:

```go
if _, ok := m[k]; ok {
    delete(m, k)
    metrics.Evictions++
}
```

The practical notes: deleting doesn't shrink the map's allocated capacity (memory isn't returned until the map is garbage), and deleting during range over the map is safe — the iteration contract allows deletion of not-yet-visited keys.

questions.question: What operations are safe on a nil map?
questions.title: Perations Are Safe On A Nil Map
questions.direct_answer: Reads (len, lookup → zero value), range (zero iterations), delete (no-op). Only writes panic.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Map Iteration And Nil.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Reads (len, lookup → zero value), range (zero iterations), delete (no-op). Only writes panic.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The full inventory, nil map on the left of each:

```go
var m map[string]int

len(m)              // 0 — safe
cap-ish size        // 0 — safe
m["key"]            // 0, false — the zero value, safe
for k := range m    // zero iterations — safe
delete(m, "k")      // no-op — safe
m["k"] = 1          // PANIC: assignment to entry in nil map
```

One operation panics; everything else answers as if the map were empty. The rule mirrors nil-map semantics generally: the map value is a pointer to the hash structure; nil points at nothing; reads and deletes can honestly report 'nothing there,' but a write needs somewhere to put the entry.

The bug pattern this creates is partial: functions that only read tolerate a nil map fine, so the defect hides until some later change adds a write. The defensive styles, in order of preference:

```go
m := map[string]int{}    // literal empty — write-ready from birth
m := make(map[string]int) // explicit
```

The empty literal is one type-safe expression that kills the whole bug class — there is no state of a map you can't write to after `m := map[string]int{}`.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The asymmetry is worth understanding rather than memorizing, because it's the same design decision appearing across Go. Consider the parallel with slices: a nil slice supports append (the allocate path creates storage on demand) — so 'var s []int; s = append(s, x)' is idiomatic. A nil map can't support 'insert on demand' for the same reason: creating a map's structure on demand would mean the write implicitly reassigns the map variable to a new pointer — but maps are passed by pointer already, and the runtime would have to reach into your variable to update it, which Go never does.

So the language's two collection types answer nil differently, each for a mechanical reason: the slice header is a value the runtime can return a new copy of (append's contract), while the map is a pointer whose replacement can only flow through assignment the caller performs. When people ask why Go is inconsistent here, that's the answer — it's not a philosophy difference, it's pointer-vs-value mechanics.

For API design, the consequence: functions that accept maps and might populate them should take-and-return (make inside, return the result) rather than fill-a-param — a nil map passed in can't be made writable from inside the function no matter what it does.

questions.question: How do you iterate a map in sorted order?
questions.title: Iterate A Map In Sorted Order
questions.direct_answer: Collect keys into a slice, sort it, range over the sorted keys — the standard pattern, since map order is deliberately random.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of Map Iteration And Nil.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Collect keys into a slice, sort it, range over the sorted keys — the standard pattern, since map order is deliberately random.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Since the language forbids relying on iteration order, deterministic iteration is a three-move pattern:

```go
keys := make([]string, 0, len(m))  // pre-sized: no growth
for k := range m {
    keys = append(keys, k)
}
sort.Strings(keys)
for _, k := range keys {
    fmt.Println(k, m[k])
}
```

Extract, sort, then walk the keys and index the map. The pre-size on the key slice matters at scale — len(m) is known, so the append loop never reallocates.

Three variations you'll meet:

sort.Strings for string keys, sort.Ints for ints; anything else gets sort.Slice(keys, func(i, j int) bool { ... }) with your comparison.

If you need value-ordered (top-N by count, say), sort the keys with a custom comparator that reads the map: sort.Slice(keys, func(i, j int) bool { return m[keys[i]] > m[keys[j]] }).

If you only need the first N sorted keys, sort a copy or use a partial approach — but profile before adding complexity; full sort of a key slice is fine at most real sizes.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why doesn't the language just offer a sorted map? Two answers: Go's map is a hash table with no order to expose (unlike a tree map), and the sorted-keys pattern composes with the sort package the language already has — the three-line idiom replaces a data structure.

The pattern's cost profile is worth knowing for performance-sensitive paths: O(n) key extraction, O(n log n) sort, then n map lookups (each O(1)). For iteration that must be deterministic at every scale, that's the honest price; the alternative (maintaining a sorted structure, like an ordered map or a B-tree keyed slice) trades O(log n) inserts for O(1) sorted walks — only worth it when sorted iteration dominates.

The standard library's own precedent: text/template sorts map keys for deterministic output — precisely so that template rendering doesn't change between runs. When your output is a diff, a hash, a golden-file test, or anything compared across executions, deterministic iteration isn't optional — the sorted-keys pattern is the fix. When it's just 'process every entry,' the random order is free and fine.
